stem: In Kafka, ordering of records is guaranteed at what level?

options.why: Order is not maintained across partitions of a topic.
Records are appended in order within one partition.
A group parallelises reads; it does not create global order.
Replicas copy a partition; they don't add ordering scope.

explanation: Kafka guarantees order only within a partition. Global ordering requires a single partition, which sacrifices parallelism.

stem: You need strict per-customer ordering with high overall throughput. What do you do?

options.text: Use one partition for the topic
options.why: Global order, but throughput is capped at one consumer.

options.text: Key records by customer_id across many partitions
options.why: Same key → same partition preserves per-customer order while partitions scale throughput.

options.text: Use null keys and many partitions
options.why: Null keys round-robin, breaking per-customer order.
Replication is durability, unrelated to ordering or parallelism.

explanation: Keying by the entity keeps its records in one partition (ordered) while other keys spread across partitions for throughput.

stem: A topic has 3 partitions and a consumer group has 5 consumers. What happens?

options.why: Within a group, a partition is owned by exactly one consumer.

options.text: 3 consumers each own a partition; 2 are idle
options.why: Parallelism is capped by partition count, so extras sit idle.
Kafka never auto-creates partitions to match consumers.
It starts fine; the extra consumers are simply unassigned.

explanation: In a group, each partition has one owner. More consumers than partitions leaves the surplus idle — add partitions to scale further.

stem: Two separate consumer groups subscribe to the same topic. Each group receives:

options.why: Splitting happens within a group, not across groups.
Every group gets every record and tracks its own offsets.
Start position depends on offset config, not group count.

options.text: Nothing until the other group commits
options.why: Groups are independent and never block each other.

explanation: Different groups each consume the whole topic independently — this fan-out is how one topic feeds many pipelines.

stem: A consumer processes a record, then crashes before committing its offset. On restart it will:

options.why: That would be at-most-once, which commits before processing.
The offset was never committed, so it re-reads — at-least-once, possible duplicate.
The data is still in the log within retention.
Nothing about offsets rebuilds a topic.

explanation: Committing after processing yields at-least-once: a crash before commit means the record is reprocessed. Make consumers idempotent.

stem: With RF=3, which setting combination best prevents data loss on leader failure?

options.why: Leader acks alone can lose data if it fails before replication.
A write needs at least two in-sync replicas, so a single failure keeps the data.
acks=0 doesn't wait for any ack; min.insync is irrelevant.
Only one replica need hold it, allowing loss on that broker's failure.

explanation: acks=all plus min.insync.replicas=2 guarantees two replicas hold each write, surviving one broker loss without data loss.

stem: Consumer lag keeps rising but consumer CPU is nearly idle. Most likely cause?

options.why: More partitions would help, not hurt, throughput.

options.text: Blocking on slow downstream calls per record
options.why: Idle CPU with rising lag points to I/O waits, e.g. slow DB/API calls, not compute.
RF affects durability/write path, not consumer throughput.
Retention affects replay window, not processing speed.

explanation: Idle CPU plus growing lag signals blocking I/O per record. Batch or parallelise downstream calls, or add partitions and consumers.

options.why: That is at-most-once — a crash loses the in-flight record.
A crash before commit reprocesses the record: no loss, possible duplicate.
Then every restart reprocesses everything within retention.
Replication is about durability, not delivery semantics.

explanation: Commit-after-processing is at-least-once. Pair it with idempotent consumers to get effectively-once cheaply.

stem: Does Kafka's exactly-once guarantee automatically extend to writes into an external database?

options.why: Kafka transactions are Kafka-to-Kafka; external systems are outside them.

options.text: No, the external sink must be idempotent or transactional
options.why: End-to-end exactly-once needs the sink to cooperate.
acks is durability of the Kafka write, not external effects.

options.text: No, exactly-once is impossible in Kafka
options.why: It exists for Kafka-internal consume-process-produce cycles.

explanation: Kafka EOS covers offsets + output topics atomically. External writes need idempotency keys or their own transactions.

stem: Consumers repeatedly rebalance under load. The most common root cause is:

options.why: Slow processing misses the poll deadline, so Kafka evicts the consumer and rebalances.
RF doesn't drive consumer group membership.
Topic count doesn't cause rebalances.
Compaction is storage-side and unrelated to group membership.

explanation: If processing a batch takes longer than max.poll.interval.ms, the broker considers the consumer dead and rebalances. Reduce batch size or raise the limit.

stem: After a consumer reads a record in a time-retained topic, the record is:

options.why: Kafka is a log, not a queue; reading doesn't delete.
Records persist for the retention window regardless of consumption, enabling replay.
Kafka has no built-in DLQ behaviour on read.
Compaction is a separate cleanup policy, not triggered by reads.

explanation: Time retention keeps records for a fixed window independent of consumption, which is exactly what makes replay possible.

stem: A team needs complex per-message routing and consumes each message once. Best fit?

options.why: Replay and partitions aren't what this workload needs.

options.text: RabbitMQ, for flexible routing and queues
options.why: RabbitMQ excels at routing keys, exchanges, and consume-once task queues.

options.text: Kafka, because it is always faster
options.why: Throughput isn't the deciding factor here; routing model is.
RabbitMQ is purpose-built for routing.

explanation: Rich routing plus consume-once semantics favour RabbitMQ. Kafka shines for high-throughput, replayable streams instead.
